verses.en: Now regarding the arrival[NOTE:1] of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered to be with him,[NOTE:2] we ask you, brothers and sisters,[NOTE:3]
notes: Or perhaps “return” (cf. CEV).
Grk “our gathering with him.”
Grk “brothers.” See note on the phrase “brothers and sisters” in 1:3.
verses.commentary:
2:1 "with regard to the coming" This is the Greek term parousia meaning "presence" or
"coming." The cultural background of the term was royal visits for which this word was
regularly employed. There are five words used in the NT to describe the Second Coming (see Special Topic below).

Here, in 2 Thessalonians there are three.

- parousia, cf. 2 Thess. 2:1,8; 1 Thess. 2:19

- epiphaneia, cf. 2 Thess. 2:8, a visible radiant coming

- apocalypsis, cf. 2 Thess. 1:6-7, meaning "an unveiling" for the purpose of revealing

The last word is also employed at the manifestation of Nero or the Anti-Christ in 2 Thess. 2:3,6,8.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SECOND COMING

SPECIAL TOPIC: NT TERMS FOR CHRIST'S RETURN

SPECIAL TOPIC: SOON RETURN

▣ "our gathering together to Him" This is a reference to

- angels gathering the saved (Matt. 13:41; 24:31; Mark 13:27; i.e. possibly referring to Jewish believers
fleeing Jerusalem as the Roman siege begins)

- the "rapture" of 1 Thess. 4:13-18 at the Second Coming

- Christians gathering together (same term used in Heb. 10:25, possibly Jesus' warning of Matt. 24:15-21;
see YouTube video by Ken Gentry, "2 Thessalonians 2. The Man of Lawlessness")

- This may refer to John 11:47-53, where "the gathering" refers to Jesus' substitutionary death and all
believers (Jew and Gentile) being brought into one group (cf. John 10:16).

Verse 3 speaks both of the saints experiencing tribulation (i.e. from unbelieving Jews and the
Roman government and of the revelation of the Man of Lawlessness. These two verses, 1 and 3, contradict
the view of a pre-tribulational, pre-millennial secret rapture of believers.

Usually Matt. 24:32-44 (cf. Luke 17:22-37) is used as support for a
secret rapture of believers while the unredeemed are left. However, in context (i.e. Matt. 24:38, Noah's day),
the unredeemed are taken to be judged. In Matt. 24:39, "took them all away" describes
those destroyed in the flood (cf. Matt. 24:37-38).

The real theological purpose of some theologians (starting with John Darby in 1830) for a
secret rapture distinct from a later, visible return of Jesus is

- to remove the tension between the imminent return of Jesus and the necessity that some prophesied
events must occur before the return

- to remove the church from earth so that the OT prophecies may be literally fulfilled to national Israel,
which is surprising in light of 1 Thess. 2:13-16 (i.e. a suffering church will not be spared an end-time persecution)

For a good discussion of the weaknesses of Dispensationalism, see the YouTube videos of Steve Gregg

- "Dispensationalism"

- "The Dangers of Dispensationalism"

- "Deconstructing Dispensationalism"

verses.zh: 我劝你们：无论有灵、有言语、有冒我名的书信，说主的日子现在（现在：或译就）到了，不要轻易动心，也不要惊慌。
verses.en: not to be easily[NOTE:1] shaken from your composure or disturbed by any kind of spirit or message or letter allegedly from us,[NOTE:2] to the effect that the day of the Lord is already here.
notes: Or “quickly, soon.”
Grk “as through us.”
verses.commentary:
2:2

NASB
"not be quickly shaken from your composure"

NKJV
"not to be soon shaken in mind"

NRSV
"not to be quickly shaken in mind"

TEV
"do not be so easily confused in your thinking"

NJB
"please do not get excited too soon"

Peshitta
"that you let not your minds be hastily excited"

REB
"do not suddenly lose your heads"

This is an AORIST PASSIVE INFINITIVE
which speaks of a mental confusion and anxiety caused by an outside agent, here
a spirit, or a message. This word literally could describe

- an earthquake

- the coming of God or the Spirit (cf. Heb. 12:26-28)

- figuratively it refers to a mental state of wavering loyalty (cf. LXX of Ps. 16:8 and Acts 2:25)

The word "quickly" implies

- Paul's surprise that so soon after he talked to the Thessalonian believers about these things
that so much confusion, fear, and speculation had occurred

- their ready acceptance of another person's opinion on this subject

It is this issue that caused Paul to write 2 Thessalonians.

▣ "or be disturbed" This is a PRESENT PASSIVE INFINITIVE
which speaks of a continuing occurrence by an outside agent, here a spirit or message. If the
first term in 2 Thess. 2:2 (i.e. "shaken") refers to their thinking process, this rare term refers to their
feelings. This term is found only in eschatological contexts (cf. Matt. 24:6; Mark 13:7).

NASB
"either by a spirit or"

NKJV, NRSV
"either by spirit or"

TEV
"by the claim. . .Perhaps this was said by someone prophesying"

NJB
"by any prediction or"

Peshitta
"nor by prophecy or the spirit"

REB
"by any prophetic utterance"

Paul lists three things (using metē three times) which
should not disturb the Thessalonian believers.

- "a spirit"

- "a message"

- "a letter"

The first is the term "a spirit" (pneumatos), used in the sense of a prophet's message
or another supernatural revelation (cf. 1 John 4:1, which relates pneuma with the Anti-Christ).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE

NASB
"or a message"

NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta
"or by word"

TEV
"or by someone preaching"

NJB
"or rumor"

This term (logos) could be rendered "by means of
someone's personal interpretation" or "by means of someone's speech."

NASB
"or a letter as if from us"

NKJV
"or by letter, as if from us"

NRSV
"or by letter, as though from us"

TEV
"Or it may have been said that we wrote this in a letter"

NJB
"or any letter claiming to come from us"

Peshitta
"nor by an epistle supposedly from us"

Paul began to personally autograph his letters to insure their
genuineness (cf. 2 Thess. 3:17). This could refer to

- someone's false interpretation of 1 Thessalonians

- Paul's preaching at Thessalonica

- a letter, supposedly by Paul, that they had recently received

▣ "to the effect that the day of the Lord has come" This is a PERFECT
ACTIVE INDICATIVE, implying "The day of the Lord had come." This whole theological issue
about eschatology was the major problem Paul was trying to clear up with this church. The remainder
of 2 Thess. 2:3-12 is an explanation as to why this statement cannot be true (cf. Matt. 24:23,26). The
events that accompany the judgment Coming had not yet begun (see Contextual Insights, C.).

There is a real tension in the NT between

- the temporal judgment on apostate Judaism within the life of the generation of Jews who heard but
rejected Jesus. This "coming" using the Roman army as God's agents of divine judgment occurred
during the Jewish War (A.D. 66-70), described so vividly by Josephus (i.e. Matt. 24;
Mark 13; Luke 17; 21).

- the final confrontation of evil and rebellion at the end of time (i.e. Gen. 3:15; Psalm 2; Ezekiel 38-39;
Daniel 2; 7; 9; 11; Zechariah 14).

verses.zh: 人不拘用甚么法子，你们总不要被他诱惑；因为那日子以前，必有离道反教的事，并有那大罪人，就是沉沦之子，显露出来。
verses.en: Let no one deceive you in any way. For that day will not arrive until the rebellion comes[NOTE:1] and the man of lawlessness[NOTE:2] is revealed, the son of destruction.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “for unless the rebellion comes first.” The clause about “the day” is understood from v. 2.

Most mss (A D F G Ψ 1175 1241 1505 M al lat sy) read ἁμαρτίας (hamartias, “of sin”) here, but several significant mss (א B 0278 6 81 1739 1881 2464 al co) read ἀνομίας (anomias, “of lawlessness”). Although external support for ἁμαρτίας is broader, the generally earlier and better witnesses are on the side of ἀνομίας. Internally, since ἁμαρτία (hamartia, “sin”) occurs nearly ten times as often as ἀνομία (anomia, “lawlessness”) in the corpus Paulinum, scribes would be expected to change the text to the more familiar term. At the same time, the mention of ἀνομία in v. 7 and ὁ ἄνομος (ho anomos, “the lawless one”) in v. 8, both of which look back to v. 3, may have prompted scribes to change the text toward ἀνομίας. The internal evidence is thus fairly evenly balanced. Although a decision is difficult, ἀνομίας has slightly greater probability of authenticity than ἁμαρτίας.
Or “the one destined for destruction.”
verses.commentary:
2:3

NASB
"Let no one in any way deceive you"

NKJV, Peshitta
"Let no one deceive you by any means"

NRSV, REB
"Let no one deceive you in any way"

TEV
"Do not let anyone fool you in any way"

NJB
"Never let anyone deceive you in this way"

This is a strong DOUBLE NEGATIVE with an AORIST
ACTIVE SUBJUNCTIVE + tis, implying a personal agency. Apparently purposeful
deception (planaō) was occurring. This is a recurrent warning in the NT, especially about
coming events (i.e. Matt. 24:4,5,11,24; Mark 13:5,6; Luke 21:8).

▣ "for it will not come unless" This is a THIRD CLASS
CONDITIONAL SENTNECE. Some events must happen first (see Contextual Insights, C.). This
coming judgment on Jerusalem and the temple was still in the future. In this context, two events are mentioned:

- the great apostasy

- the revealing of "the man of sin"

SPECIAL TOPIC: A DELAYED SECOND COMING

NASB
"the apostasy comes first"

NKJV
"the falling away comes first"

NRSV
"the rebellion comes first"

TEV
"the final Rebellion takes place"

NJB
"the Great Revolt has taken place"

Peshitta
"unless it is preceded by a rebellion"

REB
"the final rebellion against God"

This compound term literally means "to stand away from." This phrase has the DEFINITE ARTICLE,
which denotes a specific apostasy. It can be used in a negative sense (rebellion) or a positive sense (away from sin, cf. 2 Tim. 2:19). This
word was used in Greek literature (Plutarch and Acts 5:37 and Josephus) of political or military rebellion, but in the Septuagint (cf. Josh. 22:22)
and Apocrypha, it often refers to spiritual rebellion. Who is rebelling is uncertain, but they are rejecting God and His Messiah, even trying to replace Him.

The identity of those who apostacize is also uncertain. Here are some options from the NT period.

- Jewish unbelief in Jesus and their persecution of believers (i.e. 1 Thess. 2:2,14-16; Acts 17:5,13; 18:5-6; 1 Tim. 4:1-5; Rev. 1:7).

- Jewish false Messiahs (i.e. related to the fall of Jerusalem in A.D. 70, cf. Matt. 24:5) and
Jewish false prophets (cf. Matt. 7:15-23; 24:11,24) who caused the rebellion against Rome

- Roman governmental persecution (cf Matt. 24:9)

- Greek oriented false teachers (i.e. Gnostics, cf. 1 John 2:18-19; also 2 Tim. 3:1-13)

These options caused

- many loosely attached "believers" to reject the faith (i.e. Matt. 13). This rejection of "many" (cf. Matt. 24:10) may
be characterized as an apostasy within the believing community.

- Option #2 focuses on the Jewish fanatics rebelling against Rome during Nero's reign (i.e. A.D. 66).
This could be the intent of the parable in Matt. 22:2-7.

SPECIAL TOPIC: APOSTASY

SPECIAL TOPIC: QUESTIONS ABOUT JESUS' RETURN

SPECIAL TOPIC: GNOSTICISM

NASB
"the man of lawlessness is revealed"

NKJV, Peshitta
"the man of sin is revealed"

NRSV
"the lawless one is revealed"

TEV
"the Wicked One appears"

NJB
"the Rebel. . .has appeared"

REB
"wickedness will be revealed in human form"

There is a Greek manuscript variant here.

- "Lawlessness" is found in the Greek uncial manuscripts א,
B, the Coptic and Armenean translations, and the Greek texts used by Origen and Marcion (according to Tertullian)

- "Sin" is found in manuscripts A, D, F, G. K, L, P, and the Vulgate and Syriac translations and was known by
most early church fathers.

"Lawlessness" (anomias) is rare in Paul's writings (cf. Rom. 4:7; 6:19; Titus 2:14). Scribes may have
substituted the more familiar term "sin" (hamartias). The term "lawlessness" (i.e. "mystery of lawlessness")
is used in 2 Thess. 2:7.

- The UBS4 rates "lawlessness" as "almost certain" (B).

Satan is not addressed in v. 3 as he is in 2 Thess. 2:9. This refers to his yielded servant, his human
incarnation (a parody of Christ, cf. Rev. 13:1-8). Paul never used the term "Anti-Christ," but 1 John 2:18; 4:3; and
2 John 7 (written after Paul's death) refer to the same type of person. In 1 John the terms "sin" and "lawlessness" are
equated (cf. 1 John 3:4).

It is possible that Paul's "man of lawlessness" is related to the Jewish apocalyptic personification of
"the worthless one" (belial; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIAL) into a false messiah, a Satanically inspired world leader. The term may be used in this sense in

- Deut. 13:13, one who leads others away from YHWH to false gods

- 1 Sam. 2:12, one who does not know YHWH

- Nahum 1:15, personified evil

- Book of Jubilees 1:20, personified spirit

- Ascension of Isaiah, 4:18

The VERB is an AORIST PASSIVE SUBJUNCTIVE. The PASSIVE VOICE implies an outside
agent. God, not Satan, is in control of history. In God's time (cf. 2 Thess. 2:6) this parody of Christ, this incarnated evil, this servant
of Satan will be allowed to manifest himself in history (the term "reveal" was used for Christ's revelation in 2 Thess. 1:7). I believe
this refers to Nero.

The SUBJUNCTIVE MOOD does not imply that it may not occur, but confirms the ambiguous, but future,
time of the revelation (cf. 2 Thess. 2:6,8).

Notice the phrases that describe this person.

- "the man of lawlessness," v. 3

- "the son of destruction," v. 3

- "who opposes," v. 4

- "who exalts himself," v. 4

- "so that he takes his seat in the temple of God," v. 4

- "displaying himself as being God," v. 4

This person not only opposes YHWH, but tries to replace Him (i.e. claims deity, as did Nero)! The
PREPOSITION "anti" originally meant "in the place of" and later came to mean "against." Both of
these connotations fit this man of lawlessness. He wants power, control, and worship. The essence of
the Fall, human and angelic independence, is personified (cf. Dan. 11:3,16,36).

In so many ways these descriptions characterize fallen human kings and potentates (i.e. like "the
Little Horn" of Daniel 7). A good example is Nero, who I think is what Paul is referring to. Nero claimed to be the god Apollo.

NASB
"the son of destruction"

NKJV, Peshitta
"the son of perdition"

NRSV
"the one destined for destruction"

TEV
"who is destined to hell"

NJB
"the Lost One"

REB
"the man doomed to destruction"

This Hebraic idiom literally translates "the son of perdition." It was used of Judas Iscariot in John 17:12. This
future person, like Judas, will be spiritually lost and doomed to divine punishment although deeply involved in religion
(cf. 2 Thess. 2:4).

SPECIAL TOPIC: "SONS OF. . ."

verses.zh: 他是抵挡主，高抬自己，超过一切称为神的和一切受人敬拜的，甚至坐在　神的殿里，自称是　神。
verses.en: He[NOTE:1] opposes and exalts himself above every so-called god or object of worship, and as a result he takes his seat[NOTE:2] in God’s temple, displaying himself as God.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “the one who opposes,” describing the figure in v. 3. A new sentence was started here in the translation by supplying the personal pronoun (“he”) and translating the participle ἀντικείμενος (antikeimenos) as a finite verb.
Allusions to Isa 14:13-14; Dan 11:36; Ezek 28:2-9 respectively.
Grk “that he is God.”
verses.commentary:
2:4

NASB
"who opposes and exalts himself above every

so-called god or object of worship"

NKJV
"who opposes and exalts himself above

all that is called God or that is worshiped"

NRSV
"He opposes and exalts himself above

every so-called god or object of worship"

TEV
"He will oppose everything which men worship

and everything which men consider divine"

NJB
"This is the Enemy, the one who claims to be so much greater

than all that men call 'god,' so much greater

than anything that is worshiped"

These are two PRESENT MIDDLE PARTICIPLES. What is
represented here is an evil parody of Christ seeking glory and worship
(cf. Isa. 14:13-14; Ezek. 28:2; Dan. 7:25; 9:27; 11:36-37; Matt. 24:15; Mark 13:14;
see full notes at Revelation 13 online).

For a good historical overview of Nero's claims to deity and the emperor cult
that resulted, see Kenneth Gentry, Before Jerusalem Fell, pp. 271-284.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MYSTERY

▣ "exalts himself" This is the Greek compound huperairomai.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PAUL'S USE OF THE HUPER COMPOUND

▣ "so that he takes his seat in the temple of God" This phrase is often used by
those who believe that all the eschatological events mentioned by Jesus (cf. Matthew 24;
Mark 13; Luke 17; 21) or John (cf. 1 John 2; Revelation) are future events. If so, this seems to
imply a rebuilt Jewish temple, possibly along the lines of Ezekiel 40-48.

Other interpreters believe that these revealed eschatological events
were "soon" to the generation that heard Jesus speak and, therefore, must refer to historical
events of the first century Mediterranean world (i.e. Preterists).

- Caligula putting a statue of himself in the temple in Jerusalem in A.D. 40

- the fall of Jerusalem to Titus in A.D. 70

- Nero's and Domitian's reigns of terror and persecution of believers

Others of us see these eschatological events as referring to both past
first-century events and future events (Idealists). The OT prophets often took the events of their day
and projected them into a future "Day of the Lord" setting (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY). In this way the NT has a message
to its own day and every succeeding period of history. We must take seriously the historical
setting of the original author (Preterists), but also the surprising 2000 year delay of the Second Coming (Futurists).

This very specific and personal passage suggests a future personal historical
fulfillment. Yet this text is also ambiguous (possibly multiple fulfillment prophecy). Notably this kind
of language, "abomination of desolation," can refer to

- Daniel's name for this sacrilege fits the Seleucid (Antiochus Epiphanes IV)

- Roman (Titus) invasions of Jerusalem during which pagan god symbols were placed in the temple area

- this future figure also resembles the pride and arrogance of the kings of Babylon (Isaiah 14) and Tyre (Ezekiel 28)

This Greek term for "temple" (naos) was used for the Holy of Holies in
the Jewish temple, though no seat was in it. The term was also employed for pagan temples
where deities were enthroned. This may imply that the Jewish temple
must be physically rebuilt (cf. Dan. 9:24-27), possibly following Ezekiel 40-48, but not necessarily.
Remember the Jewish temple had no place to sit. It was only a Greek temple (i.e. Zeus') which had
a throne. Only modern Zionism, which is closely identified with John Darby's understanding of the
place of Israel in end-time events (i.e. Dispensationalism) requires a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem. This
seems exactly opposite of the emphasis of the book of Hebrews ("once and for all sacrifice").

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SUPERIORITY OF THE NEW COVENANT OVER THE MOSAIC COVENANT

For a good brief discussion of the modern state of Israel, see Steve Gregg's YouTube Video, "The
Modern State of Israel" or "The Dangers of Dispensationalism,"

Chrysostom interpreted "a temple" as common Pauline imagery for the
Church (cf. 1 Cor. 3:16-17; 6:19; 2 Cor. 6:16; Eph. 2:21). This view sees the man of lawlessness manifesting
himself in the visible church (i.e. a church leader). Historicists will have seen this person as the leader of the
Roman Catholic Church (also the Reformers)>

SPECIAL TOPIC: SOON RETURN

SPECIAL TOPIC: DELAYED SECOND COMING

▣ "displaying himself as being God" The lawless one actually claims deity. He is
a parody of Christ, he is Satan incarnated. This description fits Nero exactly.

In the Revelation of John there is a Satanic trinity (beast from the sea, beast
from the land, which is the false prophet, and Satan). The beast from the sea is a parody of Christ.

- has a fatal wound but is alive, cf. Rev. 13:3,14

- title "who is like the beast" reflects YHWH's description in Isa. 40:18-22; 43:11; 44:6,8,9-20; 45:6

- performed great signs cf. Rev. 13:13

- gives an identifying mark to his followers, cf. Rev. 13:16, like God's mark on Christ's followers, cf. Rev. 7:3

verses.zh: 我还在你们那里的时候，曾把这些事告诉你们，你们不记得吗？
verses.en: Surely you recall[NOTE:1] that I used to tell you these things while I was still with you.
notes: Grk “You do remember, don’t you?”
verses.commentary:
2:5 "I was telling you these things" This is an IMPERFECT TENSE signifying
that these believers had repeatedly heard preaching or teaching about this subject. They had
information about this subject that modern readers do not have (cf. 2 Thess. 2:5, "do you not remember"
and 2 Thess. 2:6, "you know"; also note 1 Thess. 3:3-4) Therefore, all modern interpretations, to some extent, are incomplete
and suppositional. Dogmatism must be avoided though careful exegesis is helpful. It is uncertain if
this phrase is referring to the information given in 2 Thess. 2:1-5 or 2 Thess. 2:6-12.

verses.zh: 现在你们也知道，那拦阻他的是甚么，是叫他到了的时候才可以显露。
verses.en: And so[NOTE:1] you know what holds him back,[NOTE:2] so that he will be revealed in his own time.
notes: Grk “and now,” but this shows the logical result of his previous teaching.
Grk “the thing that restrains.”
verses.commentary:
2:6 "you know" This implies that

- these believers knew who/what Paul was referring to because he had preached to them for a brief period

- they were currently experiencing the power/person in their lives

We must remember that the Bible was written for us, but not to us!

NASB
"what restrains him now"

NKJV
"what is restraining"

NRSV
"what is now restraining him"

TEV
"there is something that keeps this from happening now"

NJB
"what is still holding him back"

Peshitta
"what has prevented him"

REB
"the restraining power which ensures that he will be

revealed only at his appointed time"

This VERB can mean

- "hold back" (cf. Philem. 13)

- "hold fast" (cf. 1 Thess. 5:21; Luke 8:15)

- "hold away" (no biblical example)

The context favors "hold back" or "restrains." The real question is: who or what is
this restrainer? An interesting grammatical change occurs from the NEUTER in
2 Thess. 2:6,7 to the MASCULINE in 2 Thess. 2:7,8. This implies an influence capable
of personification. Because of this, at least five interpretations are plausible.

- law vs. anarchy, personified in the Roman law or empire

- angelic authority, personified in a specific angel(s), cf. Dan. 12:1; Rev. 7:1-3

- God, in the person of His Spirit or the Spirit's empowering the preaching of the gospel

- the current Roman Emperor Caludius (A.D. 41-54, whose reign limited
Nero's reign). Paul wrote Thessalonians in A.D. 48.

- The Reformers thought this was a personification of the Roman Catholic Church.

The first theory is very old and pervasive, first stated by Tertullian (A.D. 160-240).
It fits the contextual criteria that the Thessalonian Christians would have understood. Paul also spoke of
his experiences with and the benefit of law (cf. Rom. 13:1ff; Acts 17-18).

The second theory is closely related. It uses Daniel 10 as evidence for angelic
control and authority over nations (cf. LXX of Deut. 32:8) and their law systems. Daniel 12:1 mentions Michael
as a protector of God's people.

The third theory is possible because the grammar of this context uses the NEUTER
and MASCULINE forms to describe this person. The word "spirit" is NEUTER
in Greek but the Holy Spirit is a person (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PERSONHOOD OF THE SPIRIT). This would be a proof-text for Post-millennialism.

The fourth theory focuses on the time elements of the immediacy of the "coming" and
relates it to the Roman war with the Jews (A.D. 66-70). I am becoming more and more
convinced that this option fits best (i.e. Partial Preterism). For more information on this theory, read

- John Bray, Matthew 24 Fulfilled

- Kenneth Gentry, Before Jerusalem Fell

- Steve Gregg, Revelation: Four Views Revised and Updated

The spirit of the Man of Lawlessness has been in the world since Genesis 3 (cf. 1 John 2:18; 4:3;
2 John 7), but one day he will be ultimately personified. Satan does not know God's time table and possibly
has evil people ready in every age. This restraining force is ultimately under God's control and plan (cf. 2 Thess. 2:6b-7).

▣ "so that in his time he will be revealed" The person/power referred to is
apparently being controlled by God. At the appointed time in the future, he (MASCULINE)
will be allowed to manifest himself/itself. I think it refers to Nero (A.D. 54-68).

verses.zh: 因为那不法的隐意已经发动，只是现在有一个拦阻的，等到那拦阻的被除去，
verses.en: For the hidden power of lawlessness[NOTE:1] is already at work. However, the one who holds him back[NOTE:2] will do so until he is taken out of the way,
notes: Grk “the mystery of lawlessness.” In Paul “mystery” often means “revealed truth, something formerly hidden but now made widely known,” but that does not make sense with the verb of this clause (“to be at work, to be active”).

Grk “the one who restrains.” This gives a puzzling contrast to the impersonal phrase in v. 6 (“the thing that restrains”). The restraint can be spoken of as a force or as a person. Some have taken this to mean the Roman Empire in particular or human government in general, since these are forces that can also be seen embodied in a person, the emperor or governing head. But apocalyptic texts like Revelation and Daniel portray human government of the end times as under Satanic control, not holding back his influence. Also the power to hold back Satanic forces can only come from God. So others understand this restraint to be some force from God: the preaching of the gospel or the working of the Holy Spirit through God’s people.
verses.commentary:
2:7 "the mystery" God has a unified purpose for mankind's redemption that even
preceded the fall (cf. Acts 2:23; 3:18; 4:28; 17:31; Luke 22:22). Hints of this plan are revealed
in the OT (cf. Gen. 3:15; 12:3; Exod. 19:5-6; and the universal passages in the prophets). However,

This is an AORIST MIDDLE INDICATIVE meaning
God Himself has chosen believers (cf. Eph. 1:4). This is the theological opposite of
2 Thess. 2:11. The doctrine of election is

- a call to holiness (Rom. 8:28-29; Eph. 1:4), not favored standing

- not against the lost, but for the saved. It is mentioned several times by Paul in the NT
(cf. Rom. 9; 1 Cor. 7:17; Eph. 1:4-13; 2 Tim. 1:9). It is alluded to in 1 Thess. 2:12; and 5:9.

God's control of salvation and history is the focus of this context. Evil exists in the spiritual and
physical realms, but there is no dualism. Although believers cannot fully understand the mystery
of election, they have confidence that the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is in complete and loving control of all things
(i.e. John 3:16-17; 1 Tim. 2:5-6; 4:10; Titus 2:11; 2 Pet. 3:9).

Election is a wonderful doctrine. However, it is not a call to favoritism, but a call to be a channel, a tool, or
a means of other's redemption. In the OT the term was used primarily for service; in the NT it is used primarily for salvation
which issues in service. The Bible never reconciles the seeming contradiction between God's sovereignty and mankind's free will,
but affirms them both! Two good examples of the biblical tension are

- Romans 9 on God's sovereign choice and Romans 10 on mankind's necessary response (i.e. "whoever,"
"all," "everyone [twice]," cf. Rom. 10:4,11,12,13).

- Phil. 2:12-13

The key to this theological tension may be found in Eph. 1:4. Jesus is God's elect man and all are potentially
elect in Him (Karl Barth). Jesus is God's "yes " to fallen man's need (Karl Barth). Ephesians 1:4 also helps clarify the issue
by asserting that the goal of predestination is not heaven, but holiness (Christlikeness, cf. Rom. 8:28-29; 2 Cor. 5:18;
7:1; Gal. 4:19; Eph. 4:13; 1 Thess. 3:13; 4:3,7; 5:23; 1 Pet. 1:15). John 15:16 says Jesus chose us to
bear fruit! We are often attracted to the benefits of the gospel and ignore the responsibilities! God's call (election) is for
time as well as eternity.

Doctrines come in relation to other truths, not as single, unrelated truths. A good analogy would be a
constellation versus a single star. God presents truth in eastern, not western, genres. We must not remove the tension
caused by inspired dialectical (paradoxical) pairs.

The theological concept of "covenant " unites the sovereignty of God (who always takes the initiative
and sets the agenda) with a mandatory initial and continuing repentant faith response from man. Be careful of proof-texting
one side of the paradox and depreciating the other! Be careful of asserting only your favorite doctrine or system of theology.

CONTEXTUAL AND THEOLOGICAL INSIGHTS TO 2 THESSALONIANS 2:1-12

- This passage is very difficult to interpret as the numerous theories throughout church history illustrate. I would
like to quote several brief passages from my favorite books on how to interpret prophecy and apocalyptic literature.

- D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of
biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic:

- "What makes prophecy problematic? To understand the prophetic word correctly,
we must recognize that the language of prophecy may be poetic, emotive, conditional,
hyperbolic, figurative, surreal, oral and uncertain about fulfillment," p.56

- From the chart on p. 110 ‒ the function of biblical apocalyptic.

- call to worship

- comfort that God is in control

- insight into cosmic issues

- hope for the persecuted

- assurance of God's victory

- call to purity

- "The occasion and focus of most prophecy were the immediate circumstances. . .however, the
language describing the crisis. . .and the actions of God. . .is often so extreme that
some interpreters conclude it must be eschatological," p. 162

- "When determining what is metaphoric. . .every interpreter must make a conscious
effort to set aside prejudgments about eschatology. We must resist the inclination to
be controlled by a previously adopted theology of prophecy," p. 163

- Another book that has been very helpful to me in this genre is G. B. Caird, The Language
and Imagery of the Bible. Let me give you a brief quote.

"A quite different complication of the problem of identifying the referent is presented by
letters, which frequently contain allusions to previous correspondence of conversations, clear
enough to the original readers, but obscure to us (e.g. 1 Cor. 5:9; 7:1). In one of his most tantalizing
sentences Paul uses no fewer than five opaque terms ‒ 'The rebellion,' 'the man of
lawlessness,' 'the mystery of lawlessness,' 'the restraining power,' 'the restraining person,' ‒ and
adds the comment that he explained all this to his readers the last time he was with them (2 Thess. 2:3-7)." p. 11

- And, of course, I must mention what I think is the best non-technical book of "Special Hermeneutics," Gordon
Fee and Douglas Stuart, How To Read the Bible For All Its Worth, especially chapters 1, 10, and 13.

I have quoted these to whet your appetite for more study! The more you know
the more you realize there is so much more!

- Biblical Background

- Chapter 1 dealt with the temporal Coming of Christ for judgment of Jewish unbelievers. Chapters 2:1-12 deals
with the coming judgment of

- Nero

- end-time world ruler; Paul calls him "the man of lawlessness" in 2 Thess. 2:3 and "the lawless one" in 2 Thess. 2:8.

- The general background of this passage lies in the OT belief in a continuing confrontation between the
people of God and the people of the evil one (cf. Gen. 3:15; Psalm 2; 48:4-8; Ezekiel 38-39; Daniel 2; 7; 9; 11; Zechariah 14).
This conflict becomes personalized at the end time into individual leaders of both camps: God's Messiah and the Anti-Messiah
(cf. Gen. 3:15; Daniel 7; 9:23-27).

- The related passages in the NT are Matthew 24; Mark 13; Luke 17; 21;
1 Thessalonians 4-5; 1 John 2 and the book of Revelation. These passages seem to give information about

- a temporal judgment on "those who pierced Him" (i.e. unbelieving Jews who had Jesus killed and persecuted
His followers, cf. Rev. 1:7)

- a possible multi-fulfillment prophecy about the end-time. Prophetic literature often merges these two time frames.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)

- Be careful to note the "time indicators" in these passages!

- Three time elements are involved in 2 Thess. 2:1-12 (as in the Olivet Discourse and Revelation).

- current events

- future events but preceding the Second Coming

- future events concerning the Day of the Lord (
SPECIAL TOPIC: The Day of the Lord)

- It is a general principle of hermeneutics that a passage must be interpreted in light of the
immediate context (i.e. historical and literary). With this in mind, the continuing information
about the delay of the Second Coming until some events occur is crucial. There was a group
in the Thessalonica church who believed so strongly in a soon, very soon, or even Parousia past, that they
had quit work. Paul seems to address them in this discussion concerning a future coming judgment event.

The certainty of the return of Jesus is not at issue, but the "when" is! Apparently, the
church had received a "message" that the time was "now" (cf. 2 Thess. 2:2-3).

- It must be remembered that the whole subject of the return of Christ is presented
in the Bible in a dialectical tension.

- the temporal coming judgment on Jerusalem (i.e. "those who pierced Him," Rev. 1:7)

- the imminent return of the Lord contrasted with several events which must happen first. Jesus
mentioned several times that "this generation" would see His coming (i.e. Jerusalem and the temple
in A.D. 70 using the Roman army).

- Many see this chapter as apocalyptic in genre. Much of the confusion about the timing of biblical judgments is related to the
basic structure of biblical prophetic statements.

- It uses current events or crises in several ways.

- to demonstrate God's active presence and judgment in time

- to attempt to change current human actions by warning of future judgment

- The biblical writers of both prophecy and apocalyptic use highly symbolic, poetic, and hyperbolic
language that modern readers are unaccustomed to (i.e. Joel 2:25-32 compared to Acts 2:16-21).

- There is always an element of multi-fulfillment involved in this genre. The problem is, how does a modern
Bible reader know

- what is literal; what is symbolic?

- to which time period does the revelation relate?

- It seems fair to think that much of Paul's information about the coming of the Lord was taken and expanded from
Jesus' Olivet Discourse (note 1 Thess. 4:15) since I have come to believe that much of this refers to the Jewish
War with Rome that began in A.D. 66 and concluded in the destruction of Jerusalem and the
temple in A.D. 70. If this presupposition is true (and there surely is some doubt), then this chapter
relates to Jewish and Neronic persecution of believers (cf. 1 Thess. 1:6-16).

- God's judgment fell on apostate Judaism in A.D. 66-70

- God's judgment fell on the Roman Empire

- death of Nero in A.D. 68

- fall of the empire in A.D. 476
